identity.title: Test of skew (alternate cover test; vertical ocular misalignment)

technique.how: Patient fixates a target straight ahead; alternately cover one eye then the other while watching the uncovered eye for a vertical corrective refixation (one eye moves up, the other down). Any vertical re-alignment movement is skew deviation; note it may be subtle (3-20 prism diopters) and asymptomatic.
technique.prerequisites: Acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo, nystagmus, gait unsteadiness) with the patient able to fixate; performed as part of HINTS with head impulse and nystagmus assessment.
technique.contraindications: Not interpretable with pre-existing vertical strabismus, third/fourth nerve palsy, or when the patient cannot fixate.

interpretation.positive_finding: Skew deviation in acute vestibular syndrome is a central sign, most associated with brainstem (especially lateral pontine/medullary) stroke, and can identify stroke even when the head impulse test misleadingly appears peripheral.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absent skew barely lowers the probability of stroke (LR- ~0.8; sensitivity ~25%); a negative test of skew is meaningful only as part of a fully benign HINTS (abnormal head impulse, direction-fixed nystagmus, no skew).
interpretation.pitfalls: Low sensitivity - most strokes lack skew; small deviations are easy to miss without careful alternate cover; congenital or peripheral (utricular) causes of skew occur rarely. Data are from a high-risk AVS cohort examined by neuro-ophthalmology experts.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: treat as posterior-circulation stroke (MRI, stroke pathway) even if head impulse is abnormal; negative alone does not change management - rely on the full HINTS battery.

estimates.target_condition: Central lesion (stroke or other central cause) in acute vestibular syndrome - skew deviation present or untestable
estimates.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (>=1 stroke risk factor): 25 peripheral, 76 central; academic stroke center; prospective cross-sectional
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) neuroimaging plus clinical follow-up; peripheral = normal MRI and follow-up
estimates.computed_from: Table 1 reports skew present/untestable in 4% of PAVS (n=25) and 25% of CAVS (n=76) with NLR 0.78 (0.67-0.91); specificity = 1-0.04 = 0.96; LR+ = 0.25/0.04 = 6.3; prevalence = 76/101
estimates.location: Table 1 (Key clinical features in patients with peripheral versus central AVS)

estimates.target_condition: Ischemic stroke in acute vestibular syndrome - skew deviation present (untestable excluded)
estimates.population: 94 high-risk AVS patients with testable skew: 25 no stroke, 69 stroke by final imaging (2 stroke patients untestable excluded); same cohort
estimates.computed_from: Table 3 2x2: skew present 16 stroke / 1 no stroke; skew absent 51 stroke / 24 no stroke. Sens = 16/67 = 0.24; spec = 24/25 = 0.96; LR+ = 0.24/0.04 = 6.0; LR- = 0.76/0.96 = 0.79; prevalence = 69/94
estimates.quote: Skew Deviation absent 24 51 6 ... Skew Deviation present 1 16 0
estimates.location: Table 3 (Skew deviation relative to neuroimaging in AVS, stratified by h-HIT results)

sources.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009.
Tarnutzer AA, Berkowitz AL, Robinson KA, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. Does my dizzy patient have a stroke? A systematic review of bedside diagnosis in acute vestibular syndrome. CMAJ. 2011.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use skew alone to rule out stroke; do not apply HINTS outside acute vestibular syndrome (e.g., episodic or positional vertigo) or in patients who cannot fixate.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Any skew, direction-changing nystagmus, or normal head impulse in AVS is a stroke until proven otherwise; early MRI-DWI is falsely negative in ~12% in this cohort, so admit and repeat imaging if negative.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Kattah's examiners were neuro-ophthalmology-trained; no kappa reported. Accuracy of skew testing by non-expert emergency clinicians is not established in the sources reviewed.

extraction_notes: Kattah 2009 full text obtained via PMC (PMC4593511). Estimate 1 uses Table 1 (skew 'present or untestable', includes 3 untestable central cases per footnote) with the reported NLR; estimate 2 is computed from the Table 3 2x2 restricted to ischemic stroke and testable patients - both from the same cohort, so they are not independent. Footnote: two peripheral patients developed skew >1 week after onset and were not counted. Table 4 in the same paper gives the full HINTS battery: 'Dangerous bedside H.I.N.T.S. 100% 96% 0.00 (0.00-0.12)' (Table 4) - composite, not entered here. Skew 'was present in 17% of our 101 subjects' and 'evident in 4% (n=1/25) with APV, 4% (n=1/24) with pure cerebellar lesions, and 30% (n=15/50) with demonstrated structural brainstem involvement' (Results text). Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ systematic review (PMID 21576300) is cited as pooled context, but its PMC deposit is abstract-only and PubMed carries no abstract, so its pooled skew estimate could not be verified and is not entered.
